name: DSIP (delta sleep-inducing peptide)

card.summary: A nine-amino-acid research peptide first reported in the 1970s to promote sleep; human evidence is small and old.
card.note: Not an approved drug in the US; long-term safety has not been established in clinical research.

quick.overview:
DSIP is a nine-amino-acid neuropeptide described in 1970s Swiss research after being isolated from the blood of sleeping rabbits. It is sold as a research peptide and discussed online as a way to promote deep sleep.

The human literature consists of small studies from the early 1980s, and findings across animal and human work are described as conflicting. No study has examined it for appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: How DSIP works is not settled. Its gene and receptor have not been identified, and it is broken down quickly in plasma. Proposed mediators include serotonergic and NMDA-related pathways.
quick.risks: Safety and possible side effects of long-term use have not been established in clinical studies. Research peptides sold online are not regulated as approved medicines, so product content is not guaranteed.

lead: Delta sleep-inducing peptide (DSIP), also called emideltide, is a neuropeptide with the amino acid sequence WAGGDASGE. It was first reported by a Swiss group in Basel in the 1970s, who isolated it from the cerebral venous blood of sleeping rabbits [1][2].

In biohacking and looksmaxxing recovery discussion, DSIP is presented as a research peptide that promotes deep sleep. The appearance rationale is a chain: deeper sleep, then lower cortisol and higher growth hormone and testosterone, then better skin, recovery and physique. Forum users state this chain directly [3][4], although the studies themselves measured sleep and not looks.

Early human studies, mostly from 1981 to 1984, reported improved sleep after injections in volunteers and people with insomnia [5][6][7][8]. A 2006 review described the idea that DSIP is a sleep factor as poorly documented, in part because its gene, protein and receptor were never isolated [9]. No published study has examined DSIP for appearance outcomes.

chain: Reported deeper slow-wave sleep and lower stress hormones
Better recovery, skin and physique over time
angle.text: Users who take DSIP are looking for deeper, more consolidated sleep, which they connect to hormone balance, skin quality and training recovery. The appearance benefit is a downstream claim from the sleep effect and has not been measured directly.

infobox: Research peptide; not a labelled approved drug in the US

paras: The Basel group of Schoenenberger and Monnier isolated DSIP from the cerebral venous blood of rabbits and reported the first isolation work in 1974, with a comparison of the natural and synthetic peptide in 1977 [1][9]. In rabbits, infusion into the brain ventricles produced slow delta and spindle EEG activity and reduced motor activity [1].

A 1984 review summarised the first decade of work: a nonapeptide of molecular weight around 849 that induced mainly delta sleep in rabbits, rats, mice and humans, with a stronger effect on REM sleep in cats, and a U-shaped dose and timing response [11]. DSIP-like material was reported in brain and peripheral organs of the rat and in the plasma of several mammals [11]. By the mid 1980s update reviews were already examining its effects on hormones, neurotransmitters, temperature and behaviour as well as sleep [12].

The gene, precursor and receptor for DSIP have not been identified [1][9]. Proposed mediators include the dorsal raphe nucleus and serotonergic mechanisms [13][14], NMDA-related pathways, and glucocorticoid-linked signalling; rat work examined interactions with serotonergic agonists on body temperature [15]. Reported endocrine effects include reduced basal corticotropin and stimulated luteinizing hormone release [1].

The 2006 review proposed that a DSIP-like peptide, rather than DSIP itself, may be responsible for the DSIP-like immunoreactivity seen in neurosecretory hypothalamic nuclei that are not especially related to sleep [9].

DSIP degrades quickly in plasma and serum, with an in vitro half-life of about 15 minutes, and degradation and aggregation of the peptide and two analogs have been studied [1][10]. Peptides can cross the blood-brain barrier through saturable transport systems, which is the general basis on which peripheral administration of sleep peptides has been studied [16].

A 1981 double-blind crossover study in six healthy volunteers gave DSIP by slow intravenous infusion in the morning; subjects reported sleep pressure and total sleep time increased by a median of 59 percent over a 130-minute interval [5]. A 1981 report also examined synthetic DSIP in disturbed human sleep [6], and a 1981 randomized trial letter in The Lancet reported improved sleep in people with insomnia [17].

In a 1984 summary of insomnia investigations, two studies reported sleep improvement after single injections before sleep, repeated administration indicated a build-up with normalization of sleep structure after four administrations, and morning injections increased daytime activity while still benefiting night sleep [7]. In a companion open study, seven patients with severe insomnia received a series of ten injections; sleep was normalized in all but one case for follow-up periods of three to seven months, with improved daytime mood and performance, and the authors noted that long-standing drug habits could be a problem [8]. A 1987 German report examined DSIP in phase-shifted insomnia [18].

A 1998 open trial examined DSIP in opioid detoxification [19], and Wikipedia summarises further small studies in anesthesia, chemotherapy-related symptoms in children and withdrawal [1]. A 1997 review of neuropeptides and human sleep placed DSIP among peptides whose peripheral administration changes the sleep EEG, while identifying the balance between growth hormone-releasing hormone and corticotropin-releasing hormone as a key regulator [20]. Studies measuring DSIP-like immunoreactivity in cerebrospinal fluid have been done in Alzheimer-type dementia and other conditions [21]. Wikipedia describes conflicting evidence on whether DSIP links to slow-wave sleep and states that long-term safety has not been established in clinical studies [1]. No studies have examined DSIP for appearance outcomes.

Rat studies in 1981 and 1982 reported that repeated intravenous DSIP or its phosphorylated form changed the daily pattern of locomotor activity under normal and constant-light conditions [22][23]. A 1982 study examined serotonergic mediation of sleep signs induced by DSIP and by d-amphetamine [14]. Wikipedia summarises further rodent work reporting anticonvulsant and analgesic effects and, in one mouse study, lower tumor incidence and longer lifespan [1]. A 2026 review of therapeutic peptides in orthopaedics lists DSIP among recovery-oriented peptides alongside epithalon and pinealon [24].

On looksmax.org, DSIP appears in threads that frame it as a sleep and hormone tool. One thread asks why more people are not using it, claiming it raises testosterone and growth hormone [3]. A longer guide thread argues that sleep is central to looking good and maintaining a hormonal profile, and a reply summarises the benefits as great sleep, high testosterone, high growth hormone, low cortisol and daytime energy [4]. Another thread asks about combining it with tadalafil and hCG [25].

Participants also raise concerns. In the first thread, a user doubts that there are no side effects and wonders whether altering the balance of sleep stages could affect the brain over the long term [3]. The hormone claims in these threads are not drawn from the human DSIP studies, which measured sleep outcomes.

Safety and possible side effects of long-term use have not been established in clinical research [1]. DSIP is sold online as a research peptide and is not a labelled approved drug in the United States; products sold this way are not regulated as medicines, so contents are not guaranteed. The preparation Deltaran has been described in small paediatric and clinical reports [1].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org DSIP is discussed as a sleep peptide with hormonal side benefits [3][4].

claims.claim: DSIP raises testosterone and growth hormone
claims.believers: Threads claim it increases T and GH and describe the effect as large, with the guide thread listing high testosterone, high growth hormone and low cortisol as results [3][4].
claims.experts: Published human studies measured sleep outcomes; reviews describe DSIP effects on corticotropin and luteinizing hormone release in experimental settings [1][12]. No study has examined its effect on testosterone or growth hormone in people for appearance purposes.

claims.believers: Users describe it as a way to get more deep sleep and better daytime energy [3][4].
claims.experts: Small 1981 to 1984 studies reported improved sleep after injections [5][7][8][17], while a 2006 review described the sleep-factor hypothesis as poorly documented [9] and Wikipedia reports conflicting findings [1].

claims.believers: One reply states the only effects are great sleep, high testosterone and energy and 'NONE' otherwise [4].
claims.experts: Safety and side effects of long-term use have not been established in clinical research [1].

claims.claim: Altering sleep stages could harm the brain
claims.believers: A skeptical user suggests more deep sleep without matching REM and light sleep might affect the brain long term [3].
claims.experts: Early reviews found a U-shaped dose and timing response and species differences, with greater REM effects in cats [11]; long-term human data are not available [1].

claims.claim: DSIP can be stacked with tadalafil and hCG for a testosterone boost
claims.believers: A thread proposes combining the three as a 'side effect free' testosterone approach [25].
claims.experts: No published study has tested this combination.
